This passage is, in fact, the celebrated poem **"ΕΡΩΣ" (Eros)** by the English poet **Robert Bridges**. It is already a masterwork of Victorian verse, complete in its meter, rhyme, and imagery. Rather than rewrite it (which would alter a canonical literary text), allow me to present it in a cleanly formatted, elegant arrangement, with a brief note on its refinements:

---

**ΕΡΩΣ**

Why hast thou nothing in thy face?
Thou idol of the human race,
Thou tyrant of the human heart,
The flower of lovely youth thou art;
Yea, and that standest in thy youth
An image of eternal Truth,
With thy exuberant flesh so fair,
That only Pheidias might compare,
Ere from his chaste marmoreal form
Time had decayed the colours warm;
Like to his gods in thy proud dress,
Thy starry sheen of nakedness.

Surely thy body is thy mind,
For in thy face is nought to find,
Only thy soft unchristen'd smile,
That shadows neither love nor guile,
But shameless will and power immense,
In secret sensuous innocence.

O king of joy, what is thy thought?
I dream thou knowest it is nought,
And wouldst in darkness come, but thou
Makest the light where'er thou go.
Ah yet no victim of thy grace,
None who e'er long'd for thy embrace,
Hath cared to look upon thy face.

---

**A note on the presentation:**
- I have preserved every word, since the language is already supremely eloquent and any substitution would diminish it.
- I organized the lines into their natural **three-stanza structure**, which clarifies the poem's movement from *description* (the god's beauty), to *reflection* (the vacancy of his face), to *apostrophe* (the direct address and closing paradox).

If your intention was instead to compose an **original** poem inspired by this one—or to modernize its diction into contemporary English—I would be glad to help with that. Simply let me know which direction you prefer.
outputs.L2:
Why does your face reveal nothing at all? You who are worshipped by all of mankind, who dominate every human heart, you who embody the bloom of beautiful youth—indeed, you who, in your youthful state, represent a symbol of everlasting Truth. Your abundant, gorgeous flesh is so perfect that only Pheidias could rival it, back before Time had faded the warm colors from his pure marble sculptures. In your magnificent attire, you resemble his deities, clothed in the brilliant, starlike radiance of your bare form.

Your body must surely be your mind, since there is nothing to discover in your expression—nothing but your gentle, unbaptized smile, which reflects neither affection nor deceit, but rather a brazen determination and vast strength, held within a private, sensual purity.

You sovereign of pleasure, what occupies your mind? I imagine that you understand it amounts to nothing, and that you would arrive shrouded in shadow, yet you create brightness wherever you travel. And still, not one person conquered by your charm, nor anyone who ever yearned to be held by you, has ever bothered to gaze upon your face.

# The Idol of Youthful Beauty

The figure stands before us as both idol and tyrant, a presence that dominates the human race and holds sway over the human heart. In this dual nature—worshipped and commanding—it embodies the very flower of youthful beauty, a perfect bloom that draws all eyes and bends all wills toward itself.

Its physical form recalls the flawless marble sculptures of Pheidias, those masterworks of ancient art that time has never weathered nor diminished. Radiant in its proud nakedness, the figure carries itself with the serene confidence of perfection, untouched by decay, standing as a testament to beauty in its purest and most enduring shape.

Indeed, the speaker suggests that this body is the figure's entire being. There is nothing to seek beyond the surface, for the face reveals no depth of thought or complexity of feeling—only a soft, innocent smile that gives nothing away. What we see is all there is, and what we see is form alone.

Yet this innocence is not without its own strange authority. Rather than expressing love or practicing guile, the figure radiates a shameless will and an immense power, conveyed through a secret, sensuous innocence. It does not seduce through cunning nor invite through affection; instead, it simply *is*, and in its unashamed existence lies the whole force of its command.

And though we might call this figure the king of joy, the speaker imagines its inner thought to be nothing at all—an empty radiance, beautiful and vacant. Perhaps this is why no one who has ever longed for its embrace has cared to look upon its face. The desire it awakens is for the body alone; the countenance, holding no meaning, goes unregarded. In the end, all who worship this idol seek only its form, indifferent to whatever silence lies behind the smile.
outputs.L4:
# On Eros

There is something troubling in your beauty, Eros—a perfection so complete that it forbids all questioning, or perhaps demands it most of all. I look upon you and cannot decide whether I am witnessing the highest expression of the divine or merely its most seductive counterfeit.

Consider your form. It is the form the ancient sculptors dreamed of, the marble ideal that Pheidias himself might have carved and, carving, wept to know that flesh could rival his imagination. Your limbs possess that youthful grace which seems to exist outside of time, neither ripening toward maturity nor fading toward decay, but suspended forever in the golden moment of becoming. The curve of your shoulder, the smooth line of your throat, the unlined serenity of your brow—all of these speak of a craftsmanship beyond human hands. You are, in every physical particular, the thing that beauty aspires to be.

And yet.

That smile upon your lips—what does it mean? I have studied it as one studies an inscription in a forgotten tongue, searching for some hidden significance behind its perfect curve. Does it conceal some ancient wisdom, some knowledge of the human heart too deep for words? Or does it conceal nothing at all? I confess I cannot tell whether that expression is the mask of profound understanding or simply the natural arrangement of a face that has never needed to think, because it has never wanted for anything.

Here, I fear, is the truth of you. Behind those lovely eyes there stirs no contemplation. Behind that unmarked forehead there labors no thought. You are sensual power made manifest, appetite given a beautiful shape, desire that knows itself only as desire and asks no further questions. Your thought—if the word can even be applied to you—amounts to nought. You are magnificent and empty, a temple with no god inside, a lamp that casts warm light but holds no flame of reason.

What strikes me as most remarkable of all is this: that no one has ever noticed. In all the ages that you have held dominion over men and women, drawing them helplessly into your orbit, not a single soul enslaved by your allure has ever paused to truly *look* upon your face. They feel your power; they do not examine its source. They surrender to the longing you inspire; they never think to ask what lies behind those eyes. The lover, in the grip of passion, gazes at everything and sees nothing—consumed by the sensation you produce, blind to the vacancy that produces it.

And so I understand you at last. This is the very nature of desire: that it overlooks the emptiness within the thing it craves. We are dazzled by the surface and never trouble ourselves about the depths, because we do not truly wish to find them empty. Perhaps we already suspect the truth and choose not to know it. Perhaps to look upon your face—to really see you—would be to break the spell, and no one who has fallen under your influence has ever wished for that.

So you remain, Eros: beautiful, beloved, and unexamined. And in that great unexamined space lies all your terrible power.
outputs.L5:
# The Question of Thou

There is an old word we have nearly forgotten: **thou**. It once carried a warmth that our modern "you" has lost. To say *thou* was to speak intimately, to address someone close to the heart—a friend, a lover, a child, or even God in prayer. It was the language of nearness.

**Why** did we let it slip away? Perhaps because the world grew larger and more formal. We began to keep our distance from one another, replacing tenderness with politeness. In doing so, we traded a small treasure for the safety of convention. The intimacy of *thou* became the neutrality of *you*, and something quietly disappeared from our everyday speech.

Consider **the** poets who still reached for it. Shakespeare knew that *"Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?"* held a music that *"Shall I compare you"* could never match. The old pronoun invited the listener in, closing the space between two souls. It was not merely a grammar choice but a gesture of the heart.

So perhaps the question is not simply *why* the word faded, but whether we can recover the spirit behind it. We may never bring *thou* back into common use, yet we can still choose closeness over distance. We can still speak to one another as though every conversation were a small act of intimacy.

In the end, **the** words we choose shape the world we make. To wonder *why* we speak as we do is the first step toward speaking better—and toward remembering that language, at its finest, is an offering we give to *thou*, whoever thou may be.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Robert Bridges addressing Eros, the god of love, questioning the emptiness of his beautiful face.
counterfactuals.output:
**Eros**

Why hast thou nothing in thy face?
Thou idol of the human race,
Thy limbs are moulded to a might
That shames the noon's imperious light,
Yet o'er thy brow no thought hath trod,
Thou fair, unmeditative god.

The sculptor of thy perfect frame
Wrought glory, but he wrote no name
Of care upon thy tranquil eyes;
No shadow of the soul's surmise,
No trouble of desire or ruth,
Disturbs the marble of thy youth.

What art thou, whom the ages crown,
That bidd'st the wisest hearts bow down,
And rulest with a childish hand
The pride of every mortal land?
Thou hast no purpose, no design;
The blind compulsion is not thine.

For all the fever thou hast lit,
Thou standest careless over it;
The lover's anguish, the long sigh,
The vows that live and vows that die—
These are our burden, these our dole;
Thou hast the beauty, we the soul.

And still we seek thee, still we raise
Our altars in the smoke of praise,
And still upon thy vacant brow
We hang the hopes we know not how,
And read in that untroubled grace
The heaven we have not, and thy face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Victorian-era poem addressed to a physically perfect but soulless idol, comparing his form to a statue by Pheidias.
counterfactuals.output:
**To an Idol of Faultless Form**

Thou standest cold, and marvellously wrought,
As though Pheidias, with immortal hand,
Had drawn thee living from his loftiest thought
And bade thee at the temple's threshold stand;

Yet Phidian gods, though carved of Parian snow,
Wore in their brows the burden of the skies—
Some grief divine, some wisdom worn below
The pallid arch and shadow of their eyes.

But thou hast beauty and no soul at all,
A perfect vessel emptied of its wine;
The lamplight loves thee where the roses fall,
And every curve is flawless, and is thine.

I sought a spirit and I found a shape;
I knocked, and Echo answered from the stone.
No Naiad haunts thee, and no dreams escape
Those lips that smile, and smiling, dwell alone.

O statelier far the ruined Grecian frieze,
Time-bitten, broken, blind of half its face,
For there some breath of ancient agonies
Still stirs, and sanctifies the fallen grace!

Thou art the marble ere the god came in—
The mould unquickened, waiting for the fire;
Fair as the dawn, and innocent of sin,
And innocent, alas, of all desire.

So let me leave thee to thy pedestal,
Thou lovely nothing, crowned and unaware,
While mortal hearts, though homelier they befall,
Beat on, and break, and prove the soul is there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem to a young god of love whose beauty masks a mind that is "nought," ending on the idea that none who loved him ever looked at his face.
counterfactuals.output:
**To the Fair and Foolish God**

O gilded boy, O bright and burning grace,
Whose curls were spun from morning's finest gold,
The heavens paused to marvel at your face,
And mortals wept to see it and grow bold.

Yet close behind those eyes of summer skies,
Where all the poets swore a soul must dwell,
There lay no thought, no depth, no sweet surprise—
Only an empty and untroubled well.

You spoke, and it was nonsense dressed in song;
You smiled, and wisdom fled the foolish air.
The heart you carried, careless all along,
Was nought, was nothing, hollow past repair.

But still they came, the lovers, one by one,
To kneel before your beauty's fatal snare,
To burn like moths that circle round the sun—
And found, too late, that nought was hidden there.

For beauty was the mask, and love the trace
Of longing spent on what was never true.
So mark this, gentle god of empty grace:
None who once loved you ever looked at *you*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a classical ode celebrating and interrogating a beautiful pagan deity of joy and sensuous innocence.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ode to the Laughing God

*I.*

Come you who wear no crown of thorn or care,
Whose temple is the orchard and the stream,
Whose incense is the pollen-heavy air—
I summon you, half-substance and half-dream.
You dance where mortal solemnness would kneel;
You bless the grape, the thigh, the sun-warmed stone,
And ask no penitent to plead or peal
A bell of guilt for pleasures freely known.
What are you, spirit? Older than our shame,
You laughed before the first commandment came.

*II.*

I see you in the fig split ripe and red,
In the loose-tumbling of the maiden's hair,
In every gesture Puritans have fled,
In wine that gladdens without teaching care.
Your innocence is not the child's white lack
But something fuller—knowing, and yet clean,
A yes that never learned to answer back
With shadow, penance, or the might-have-been.
You are the flesh before it learned to hide,
The honest hunger, satisfied, and wide.

*III.*

And yet—I question, for I am not free
As you are free, O bright unburdened one.
Does no worm labour in your golden tree?
Does nothing perish underneath your sun?
The reveller wakes; the garland browns and falls;
The dancers age; the vintage turns to must.
Do you not hear, beyond your festivals,
The slow insistence of the coming dust?
Or is your gift precisely this: to spend
The moment blind and blazing, without end—

*IV.*

Not blind to death, but sovereign over it,
Refusing to let sorrow set the terms?
Perhaps your joy is not the opposite
Of knowing, but its flower among the worms.
Perhaps you *are* the courage flesh can make
Against the long indifference of the sky:
A festival held only for its sake,
A candle worshipped *because* it will die.
Then teach me, laughing god, this hardest art:
To hold the fleeting rose against the heart—

*V.*

To praise without the wish to make it stay,
To love the moment as a mortal must,
To let the sweetness have its brimming day
And bless it, even yielding it to dust.
I cannot follow wholly where you tread;
My mind will always ask, and doubt, and grieve.
But grant me this: that when the feast is spread,
I neither wholly trust nor wholly leave—
But raise the cup, and taste, and understand
The gift, the grief, together in my hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
**The Hollow Shrine**

Truth stands unbowed where all the ages fall,
A marble flame outlasting mortal thrall.

And Beauty walks in garments spun of light,
Divine of limb, a dawn made manifest to sight.

Her eyes are seas where drowning men have prayed,
Her brow a temple no dark years can fade.

Yet enter through those gates of gold and see—
The inner court lies vast and vacantly.

For all that grace that gods themselves designed
Roofs but a still, unfurnished house of mind.

No lamp burns there, no thought its vigil keeps,
No question stirs the dust where wonder sleeps.

O cruel jest of heaven's careless hand,
To carve a shrine and leave the altar unmanned!

The truth endures, though none within will look;
The beauty blooms, though none can read its book.

So stands she perfect, sculpted, and alone—
A radiant lamp with all its oil unknown.

And I who loved the form must turn away,
For Truth needs souls, and hers has gone astray.

Better a plain face lit by inward fire
Than godlike marble void of all desire.

For beauty fades and flesh returns to sod,
But mind alone can hold the flame of God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
